pregon.title:
One speech,

four voices.
pregon.intro: The 2026 festival speech of the Brotherhood of San Pedro de Alcántara. An AI-created audiovisual piece in which the speaker talks live with the Marquis of Duero, Saint Peter of Alcántara and his own father, in front of the whole town.

meta.label: Context
meta.value: Festival speech of the Brotherhood of San Pedro de Alcántara (Marbella)

meta.label: Role
meta.value: Direction, production and post-production · AI video

meta.label: Tools
meta.value: Magnific · Seedream 5.0 Pro · MiniMax H3 · Creatify Aurora · ElevenLabs · Claude · CapCut

player.intro: Experience the piece as the speaker did: at each pause the scene waits while he speaks, until you decide to continue.
player.videoLabel: Video of the speech with the three characters

loops.text: My General, you who laid out this delta with irrigation channels, roads and sugar cane, you who dreamed of the Farm School to redeem the land through science... What do you feel, seeing that the fields are today squares, seafront promenades and the home of thousands of people from all over the world? Does the loss of the agricultural utopia pain you, or are you proud to see what your seed has become?

My General, allow me to go back for a moment. Before asking you about what you see today, I would like to ask you about what you dreamed of back then. Why San Pedro? What led you to build an agricultural colony here? What did you imagine this place would become when you decided to set your project in motion?
That June afternoon at Monte Muro, a bullet took your life and San Pedro lost its guardian. When you fell on the battlefield... did you think of your colony?
And yet, my General, a town's battles never truly end.
Yes, my General. Even today there is one option still standing, without uniform or sword, fighting on the front line every day for this town you dreamed of.
Friar Peter... you who sought the most hidden corner of the world to go barefoot, you who fled from honours... What does your heart tell you, seeing that your name blossomed here, by the sea?

Friar Peter, I left San Pedro as a child. I went away when I was six, and for a long time I thought I had lost my town. It took me many years to understand that perhaps one never loses the place one belongs to. Tell me, why do you think some of us can leave a place and yet spend a whole lifetime trying to return to it?

Friar Peter, they say Francis of Assisi had a gift. He knew how to look at his people and see what they truly needed. And he gave it back to them as the Gospel, without adornment. You learned from him, in a time of wealthy convents and a faith weighed down with stone and gold. What did those people lack, that you chose to give them by walking barefoot? And today, with so much noise, so much haste... what do you think ours lacks?
What advice would you give this Brotherhood and the people of San Pedro in the 21st century?

notes.text: And so there was, my General.

assignment.heading: The Brief
assignment.quote: The challenge: letting three characters tied to the town talk with the speaker, live and in front of everyone.
assignment.p1: The Brotherhood of San Pedro de Alcántara's 2026 speaker contacted me directly with a clear idea. He wanted a journey through the town with three stops. At each one a character would appear, he would ask them questions live from the stage, and the character would answer him on screen.
assignment.p2: There was one non-negotiable requirement: the three characters. Two are historical figures tied to the town's identity, the Marquis of Duero and Saint Peter of Alcántara. The third is the speaker's father, who was meant to give this very speech in 2004 and couldn't. That scene was the heart of the project and set its bar, because part of the audience knew that face and his son would be standing right there.

live.heading: Designing for a live event
live.quote: A video can't guess how long someone will take to speak.
live.p1: The core problem wasn't visual, it was timing. The speaker would be talking live, and each turn could last twenty seconds or two minutes depending on the emotion of the moment or the audience's reaction. With a continuous video he would have had to rush or fill silences.
live.p2: The solution was to split the piece into three blocks, one per character, and present it as a sequence of slides. Every time the speaker talks, the scene loops: the character stays on screen, alive but waiting, until the speaker finishes and moves on. That way he sets the pace, not the video.
live.p3: A few days before the speech we met at the church to test all the audio and video equipment in the real space. On the day, there wasn't a single technical issue.

steps.text: The speaker asks from the stage
The scene loops while he speaks, at his own pace
One click and the character answers

characters.heading: The Characters
characters.quote: Three characters who, together, tell the town's story: the one who founded it, the one who named it and the one who lived it.
characters.p1: The three characters weren't chosen at random. The Marquis of Duero founded the town, Saint Peter of Alcántara gave it its name and the speaker's father stands for the people who have lived it. Making them speak was making the town itself speak.
characters.p2: I followed the same method with all three. First I gathered all the available visual material. Then I translated it into a photographic face with Seedream 5.0 Pro. Finally I locked that face into a character sheet (the same face from several angles and with several expressions). It works like an actor's casting card: before generating a single shot, the character is already defined. It's the key piece, because AI video tools tend to “forget” a face from one clip to the next, and the sheet is the reference that prevents it.

items.name: The Marquis of Duero
who: Manuel Gutiérrez de la Concha e Irigoyen (1808-1874), first Marquis of Duero, is the person San Pedro Alcántara owes its existence to as we know it. A soldier and politician, in 1860 he founded an agricultural colony built around growing sugar cane. It became the most important agricultural colony in Spain in the second half of the 19th century, and the largest ever created by private initiative.

He named it in honour of his favourite saint and of his mother, Petra de Alcántara Irigoyen. Under his drive came the sugar mill, which saved carrying the cane all the way to the mills in Málaga, and the church that became the town's parish. He died in 1874, mortally wounded at the battle of Monte Muru, during the Third Carlist War. Today the town's main avenue bears his name.
approach: He opens the journey, in the town of his time. I started from several illustrations of him. Each one interprets him in its own way, so the work was to keep the features that repeated and turn them into a believable photographic face, that of a 19th-century soldier. His voice comes from the ElevenLabs library.

items.name: Saint Peter of Alcántara
who: He was born in Alcántara (Cáceres) in 1499 and died in Arenas de San Pedro (Ávila) in 1562. A Franciscan friar, reformer and driving force behind the Discalced movement, he was an important figure of 16th-century Spanish spirituality. Today he is the patron saint of Extremadura.

His life was marked by austerity and penance. He founded El Palancar, near Pedroso de Acim, known as the smallest convent in the world. He wrote a short treatise on prayer that was translated into every European language. He was also a support and spiritual director to Saint Teresa of Ávila, whom he advised in her reform of the Carmelites.
approach: There are no photographs of the saint, only the image that painting and sculpture have passed down over the centuries. That's why his face starts from illustrations and statues, which is how the town knows him.

I placed him in El Palancar because that small convent sums up his way of seeing life better than any explanation. The quill, a nod to his writings, and the dove are woven into the scene naturally, without underlining them. Those who know his iconography recognise them; those who don't see a coherent scene.
His voice belongs to a real person, chosen by the speaker and used with their explicit permission.
items.sheetAlt: Character sheet of Saint Peter of Alcántara: the barefoot friar, in habit and Franciscan cord, from several angles
frameAlts: Saint Peter of Alcántara looks at the camera through an opening in a stone wall
Saint Peter of Alcántara, from behind, in a bare cell with a wooden cross on the wall
Saint Peter of Alcántara holds a quill and a book under the convent's beams
Saint Peter of Alcántara writes with a quill beside a white dove

items.name: The father
who: In 2004, the speaker's father was due to give the Brotherhood of San Pedro de Alcántara's speech. A health problem prevented him. Twenty-two years later, his son, now the speaker himself, wanted to pay tribute to him by finishing that speech together. That's why his appearance isn't an effect, but the closing of something left unfinished.
approach: He was the most delicate character and the one that set the bar for the whole project. In the other two cases, the reference was an artistic interpretation. Here it was a real person, whose face his family and neighbours would recognise.

The face was rebuilt by combining old photographs with frames from family videos. The videos brought what a photo lacks: gesture, and the face in motion. His scene takes place in the town's present-day church and its square.

The voice was the biggest challenge. We tried to rebuild it from fragments of audio and video, but the result wasn't good enough. I talked it over with the speaker and we decided his father would speak with his son's voice. With a likeness that left no room for error, we preferred a meaningful voice to an imperfect imitation. That decision ended up giving the scene a meaning of its own: father and son sharing, at last, the same speech.
items.sheetAlt: Character sheet of the speaker's father: dark suit and glasses, from the front, in profile and from behind

settings.heading: The Settings
settings.quote: The concept was a journey: the places had to be as much protagonists as the characters.
settings.intro: I generated each setting without characters and treated it like a film set, with period, light and detail resolved before putting anyone in front of it. That way each place stands on its own and the character only has to inhabit it.

items.name: The town in the past
items.body: This is the Marquis of Duero's scene. I rebuilt different corners of San Pedro Alcántara from old photographs taken in different eras. Since each photo shows the town at a different moment, light and style had to be unified so every place would feel part of the same town.
alts: The town church among palm trees, in 19th-century San Pedro Alcántara
Farmland with the village and its church in the background
Street of whitewashed houses with neighbours at their doors and the bell tower in the background

items.name: The El Palancar convent
items.body: This is Saint Peter of Alcántara's scene, in the convent he founded in Cáceres. A tiny, austere space where the set says as much as the character.
alts: Inside the El Palancar convent: wooden beams, stone walls and a cross beside a small window

items.name: The church and its square
items.body: This is the father's scene, recreated from current photographs of the church and the square. The journey ends in the present, in the very place where the audience was sitting while watching the piece.

process.heading: The Process
process.quote: A project from start to finish, with one person at the helm.

steps.title: Research and documentation
steps.body: It all started with gathering material: illustrations and statues for the historical characters, old photographs of the town, current images of the church and the convent, and the speaker's family archive. Without this phase no likeness is possible, historical or family.

steps.title: Structure
steps.body: I organised the piece into three blocks, one per character: the Marquis, Saint Peter and the father. Each one's questions were settled with the speaker before production began.

steps.title: Characters
steps.body: I generated each face with Seedream 5.0 Pro and locked it into its character sheet before moving to video.

steps.title: Settings
steps.body: I generated each place separately, like a film set.

steps.title: Composition
steps.body: I placed each character into their setting, using their character sheet as a reference to keep the face consistent.

steps.title: Animation
steps.body: I animated the images with MiniMax H3. I wrote every prompt in cinematic language: shot type, lens, light and camera movement, just as you would explain it to a director of photography.

steps.title: Voices
steps.body: I created the three voices in ElevenLabs: one from its library for the Marquis, a real person's voice, with their permission, for Saint Peter, and the speaker's own voice for his father.

steps.title: Lip-sync
steps.body: I synced each character's mouth to their voice using Creatify Aurora.

steps.title: Editing and loops
steps.body: I edited the three blocks in CapCut and prepared the looping scenes that keep each character waiting while the speaker talks. The final piece was presented as a sequence of slides, so he could move forward with a click.

steps.title: Technical test
steps.body: A few days before the speech we met at the church to test the audio and video in the real space.

process.note: I used Claude as cinematic support, together with installed skills to translate each scene into prompts in directing language. The idea, the production and the creative decisions were mine, with input from the speaker.

onStage.heading: Live
onStage.videoTitle: Recording of the speech · RTV Marbella
onStage.credit: Recording of the speech: RTV Marbella · Video published on YouTube by OSP
onStage.p1: On 26 September the piece was screened during the speech. The audience was surprised by the staging, and the father's appearance on screen moved the speaker and his family.
onStage.closingHeading:
From idea to screen,

from start to finish.
onStage.closingP1: This project taught me to take a complete audiovisual piece from start to finish on my own and to build my own process, from research to the creation of characters and settings, production and editing.
onStage.closingP2: It also confirmed something I bring from UX: you design for whoever is going to use it. Here it was a speaker facing his town, and what he needed wasn't a perfect video, but control over time.

pregon.sources: The historical facts in the Marquis and saint sections have been checked against the Biographical Dictionary of the Spanish Royal Academy of History and a University of Málaga thesis on the agricultural colony.

dailynook.title:
Where specialty coffee

is lived without rush, among the coffee fields.
dailynook.intro: Daily Nook Coffee · The Nook Grounds — a resort for specialty coffee lovers set in the coffee estates of Colombia.

concept.heading:
The

Concept
concept.quote: The challenge: turning a passion —specialty coffee— into a place to stay and live it.
concept.p1: Daily Nook Coffee is my final project for the UX/UI Specialist Course at La Hauss. The brief: design the site for a resort meant to be lived in, with tiered stays, a simple booking process and a concept that's clear from the first scroll.
concept.p2: I chose to aim it at people for whom coffee doesn't taste like routine, but like ritual. That's how The Nook Grounds came about: a century-old Colombian coffee estate reinvented as a slow living sanctuary, built among the coffee fields, where guests don't just stay —they taste, learn and live specialty coffee from start to finish.
concept.p3: To meet the brief's requirements I designed the mandatory views —header and footer, home, the tiers category, the stay article and the booking checkout— and delivered them as a navigable prototype in its three versions: mobile, tablet and desktop, without forcing users to register in order to book.

research.heading: The Research
research.intro: Before designing a single screen, I spent time understanding who I was speaking to and what I was competing against. This phase defined two proto personas, a benchmark of three references and the site map that structures the whole navigation.

personas.name: Sofía Cortés
personas.quote: I don't want coffee to wake up. I want coffee to stop.
personas.profile: A perfectionist and an introvert. She values minimalist aesthetics, sustainability and quality over quantity. Her coffee is the only sacred moment of the day.
personas.goals: Escape urban noise and hyperconnection, feel cared for without being intruded upon, and enjoy coffee as a pleasure, not as fuel.
personas.frustrations: Massive, noisy hotels, strict breakfast schedules and forced tourist activities with crowds.

personas.name: Mateo Gusto
personas.quote: I'm here to understand the science behind the magic.
personas.profile: A methodical, self-taught coffee nerd. He perfects his pour-over on weekends and knows roasting theory, but has never set foot on a farm.
personas.goals: Validate his knowledge with practice: roast his own coffee, understand the process and talk to the people who grow the bean.
personas.frustrations: Superficial tourist tours, poorly extracted coffees that claim to be specialty, and the lack of transparency about the product's origin.

benchmark.name: Finca Rosa Blanca
benchmark.pro: Minimalist, clean design with good use of space. Clearly identifies each tier and its price, uses breadcrumbs and filters, and shows a booking summary.
benchmark.con: The external booking engine breaks visual consistency, the breadcrumbs aren't clickable and the calendar doesn't make the status of each date clear.

benchmark.name: Aquiares
benchmark.pro: A hero that quickly communicates who they are and what they offer, a clean design and the booking status visible at all times. Lets you go back to the previous step.
benchmark.con: Redirects to an external page that breaks the flow, missing breadcrumbs, confusing button hierarchy and no room information.

benchmark.name: Hacienda Venecia
benchmark.pro: A relevant CTA from the start, photos of the stay, modals with information and the main features shown visually.
benchmark.con: A very poor booking form with no booking engine, missing breadcrumbs, mixed languages and booking information that doesn't stay visible.

design.heading: The Design
design.p1: With the research clear, I built a visual system that breathes the coffee's origin: earth tones and coffee-field green, an editorial typeface with character and warm, handcrafted iconography.
design.p2: The style guide brings together colour, typography and icons. From it I built a component library —navigation, cards, calendar, forms and the service icons— to keep everything consistent from the home to the checkout.
design.styleGuideAlt: Daily Nook Coffee — style guide: colour, typography and icons
design.tiersIntro: Three packs that scale with how deep you go into the world of coffee —from absolute silence to mastering the craft—. Each level steps up the accommodation, barista equipment and experiences, and can be booked without registering.

tiers.name: The Ritual of the Pause
tiers.desc: Absolute disconnection in an intimate adobe cabin: filter coffee you brew yourself (V60) and sensory rituals on your private porch.

tiers.name: The Alchemy of Origin
tiers.desc: A sensory immersion in a historic loft in the old drying house: espresso machine, micro-lots and guided experiences such as the Origin Tour and the Sunset Cupping.

tiers.name: The Master's Legacy
tiers.desc: Total mastery in a suite with fireplace and panoramic terrace: a La Marzocco GS3 machine, the rarest coffees and 100% private experiences, including roasting your own batch.

design.checkoutIntro: The booking is resolved in four steps, without forcing users to register and with breadcrumbs present at all times so they always know where they are and can go back. The goal: the fewest possible frictions between desire and booking.

checkoutSteps.title: Pack and dates
checkoutSteps.body: The user sees the selected pack and can change it, choose check-in and check-out dates and the number of guests.

checkoutSteps.title: Extras
checkoutSteps.body: Add additional services and experiences to personalise the stay before moving on to payment.

checkoutSteps.title: Payment
checkoutSteps.body: Enter the payment details to confirm the booking, with the order summary always in view.

checkoutSteps.title: Thank you page
checkoutSteps.body: A confirmation page closes the flow and recaps the booking with all its details.

responsive.label: Responsive prototype · mobile, tablet and desktop

prototype.heading:
A prototype

for living coffee.
prototype.p1: The result is a navigable Figma prototype in its three versions —mobile, tablet and desktop—, consistent from the home to the payment.
prototype.p2: Beyond the screens, this project forced me to think like a product designer: start from real research, justify every decision with the site map and make sure the experience —like a good cup of coffee— is enjoyed without rush. It's the closing piece of the UX/UI Specialist Course at La Hauss and the one that best explains how I work.

alfonso.title:
When starting

your own firm begins with a

blank screen.

challenge.heading:
The Starting

Point
challenge.quote: The problem wasn't his reputation as a lawyer. His digital presence needed a boost.
challenge.body: Alfonso López had practised law for years, but always under another firm's umbrella. No logo, no visual identity, no website and no online presence beyond the clients he had worked with before. His network existed, but in the digital world he was invisible. And on the Costa del Sol, one of the most saturated legal markets in Spain, that's a serious problem.

strategy.heading: The Strategy:<brSm></brSm> Winning by Design
strategy.intro: The websites of most lawyers on the Costa del Sol share a pattern: outdated, text-heavy and with a design that hasn't changed in ten years. That, rather than a problem, was our biggest opportunity. The strategy rested on three key decisions:

items.title: Identity from scratch
items.body: Before touching the website, we worked together on the logo and the corporate colour palette. He needed an image that conveyed seriousness without feeling cold, and that worked equally well on a business card and on a digital banner.

items.title: Minimalist, clean design
items.body: Against the visual noise of the competition, we chose a website with plenty of space, clear typography and direct navigation. So that in five seconds the user knew what Alfonso does, how he can help and how to reach him.

items.title: SEO foundations from day one
items.body: In a competitive market, showing up on Google isn't optional. I structured the content and the code with ranking in mind from the start, and we worked on the first blog articles to begin building authority on relevant searches.

development.heading: The Development
development.p1: We built it in WordPress, with an architecture designed so Alfonso could manage the content on his own without depending on me for every minor change.
development.p2: I implemented clear CTAs at the site's strategic points and a contact form accessible from any page, because in a law firm every enquiry is a potential client.
development.p3: All the code was optimised for load speed and mobile, which is how most people look for a lawyer today. The website wasn't launched and forgotten: we keep working together to improve ranking, add new content and adjust whatever the data calls for.

result.heading:
An identity of his own

in a saturated market.
result.p1: Alfonso went from not existing online to having a coherent, professional and distinctive digital presence. He has his own brand image, a website he can proudly show any client and a platform that works for him around the clock.
result.p2: What satisfies me most about this project isn't the visual result, but the starting point: building something from scratch alongside someone betting hard on their own path has a different value. Projects like this require me to understand the client's business before touching the design, and that's exactly what I look for in every brief.
